decks.title: Motion in One Dimension — Part 1: Describing motion and its graphs
goals: Distinguish scalars from vectors and distance from displacement
Calculate average speed, average velocity and acceleration, and explain retardation
Read distance-time and velocity-time graphs for speed, acceleration and displacement

slides.heading: Describing motion
slides.body_md: Part 1 — to describe a journey we need to say how far, how fast and whether the speed is changing.

visual.alt: Flow: distance and displacement, speed and velocity, acceleration, graphs

slides.narration: This part builds the vocabulary of motion along a straight line. We separate distance from displacement, speed from velocity, and then read all of it from graphs.

slides.heading: Scalars and vectors
slides.body_md: A **scalar** has magnitude only. A **vector** has magnitude **and direction**. A body is **at rest** if its position does not change with time and **in motion** if it does.

visual.alt: Table of scalar quantities and the matching vector quantities

slides.narration: Distance, speed, mass and time are scalars, because a number and a unit describe them fully. Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors, because the direction matters as well.

slides.heading: Distance and displacement
slides.body_md: **Distance** is the **total length of the path** travelled (a scalar). **Displacement** is the **shortest straight-line distance from the start to the end, in the direction from start to end** (a vector). A school bus goes 8 km north and then 3 km back.

slides.body_md: A boy walks 40 m north and then 30 m south along the same straight road.

visual.alt: Table giving the two legs of a boy’s walk

slides.narration: A boy walks forty metres north and then thirty metres south. What is his displacement?

slides.heading: Worked example 1: distance and displacement
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** For the bus journey find the distance, the displacement and the final position from the depot.

**Step 1.** Distance $= 8 + 3 = 11$ km.

**Step 2.** Displacement $= 8 - 3 = 5$ km towards north.

**Step 3.** For a body that returns to its starting point, the displacement is zero although the distance is not.

visual.alt: Table of the distance and displacement of the bus journey

slides.narration: Add the lengths to get the distance. Subtract the return leg from the outward leg to get the displacement, and state its direction. If a body comes back to its start, its displacement is zero.

slides.heading: Speed, velocity and uniform motion
slides.body_md: **Speed** = distance ÷ time (scalar); **velocity** = displacement ÷ time (vector). Motion is **uniform** if equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, however small, and **variable** otherwise. **Average speed** = total distance ÷ total time.

visual.alt: Table of speed, velocity and average speed with their formulae and units

slides.narration: Speed is distance divided by time and velocity is displacement divided by time. Both are measured in metres per second. When the speed changes, we use the average speed, which is the total distance divided by the total time.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: average speed
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A delivery rider covers 900 m in 180 s and then 1500 m in 420 s. Find the average speed for the whole journey.

**Step 1.** Total distance $= 900 + 1500 = 2400$ m.

**Step 2.** Total time $= 180 + 420 = 600$ s.

**Step 3.** Average speed $= \dfrac{2400}{600} = 4$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the distance and time of the two parts of the rider’s journey

slides.narration: Do not average the two speeds. Add the distances, add the times, and divide the total distance by the total time. Here twenty four hundred metres in six hundred seconds gives four metres per second.

slides.heading: Quick check: average speed
slides.body_md: Add the distances and the times first.

visual.alt: Table of two parts of a run

slides.narration: A runner covers one hundred and twenty metres in twenty seconds and then eighty metres in thirty seconds. What is the average speed?

slides.heading: Acceleration and retardation
slides.body_md: **Acceleration** is the **rate of change of velocity**: a = (v − u) ÷ t, in m s⁻². If the velocity falls, the acceleration is **negative** and is called **retardation** (or deceleration).

visual.alt: Table of the acceleration and retardation of a scooter

slides.narration: Acceleration tells us how fast the velocity changes. A positive value means speeding up. A negative value means slowing down, and we call its size the retardation.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: acceleration
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A train starting from rest reaches 30 m s⁻¹ in 2 minutes. Find its acceleration.

**Step 1.** $u = 0$, $v = 30$ m s⁻¹, $t = 2 \times 60 = 120$ s.

**Step 2.** $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{30 - 0}{120} = 0.25$ m s⁻².

visual.alt: Table of the data and answer for the train

slides.narration: Convert the time to seconds first. The velocity changes by thirty metres per second in one hundred and twenty seconds, so the acceleration is one quarter of a metre per second squared.

slides.heading: Quick check: acceleration
slides.body_md: Use the change in velocity divided by the time.

visual.alt: Table giving initial and final velocity and the time

slides.narration: A car changes its velocity from ten to twenty five metres per second in five seconds. What is its acceleration?

slides.heading: Distance-time graphs
slides.body_md: On a **distance-time graph**: a **horizontal line** means the body is **at rest**; a **straight sloping line** means **uniform speed**, and the **slope = speed**; a **curve** means **variable speed**.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: reading a velocity-time graph
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** The graph shows a tram: it speeds up from rest to 12 m s⁻¹ in 6 s, keeps this velocity for 4 s and stops in 3 s. Find the acceleration in the first 6 s and the total distance.

**Step 1.** $a = \dfrac{12 - 0}{6} = 2$ m s⁻².

**Step 2.** $S_1 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 = 36$ m, $S_2 = 4 \times 12 = 48$ m, $S_3 = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 3 \times 12 = 18$ m.

**Step 3.** Total distance $= 36 + 48 + 18 = 102$ m.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector and never exceeds the distance.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time; acceleration = (v − u) ÷ t; negative acceleration is retardation.
Slope of a distance-time graph = speed; slope of a velocity-time graph = acceleration.
Area under a velocity-time graph = displacement.

visual.alt: Summary table of what the slope and area of each graph give

slides.narration: To sum up. Distance is a scalar and displacement is a vector. Average speed uses total distance and total time. The slope of a distance time graph is speed. The slope of a velocity time graph is acceleration, and its area is displacement.

slides.heading: Exam tips: Part 1
bullets: Write the direction with every displacement, velocity and acceleration.
Convert km per hour to m per second and minutes to seconds before substituting.
For an area on a graph, split the shape into triangles and rectangles.
Write the unit of every answer.

goals: Derive v = u + at, S = ut + ½at², S = ½(u + v)t and v² = u² + 2aS from a velocity-time graph

slides.heading: Equations for uniform acceleration
slides.body_md: Part 2 — one straight line on a velocity-time graph gives all four equations of motion.

visual.alt: Flow: velocity-time graph, four equations, free fall

slides.narration: When the acceleration is uniform, the velocity time graph is a straight line. From that single line we can derive every equation of motion. We then use them for bodies falling freely.

slides.heading: Derivation 1: v = u + at
slides.body_md:
The body starts with velocity $u$ and has velocity $v$ after time $t$. The slope of the line is the acceleration:

$a = \dfrac{v - u}{t}$, so **$v = u + at$**.

slides.heading: Derivation 2: S = ut + ½at²
slides.body_md:
The distance $S$ is the area under the line: a rectangle $u \times t$ plus a triangle $\dfrac{1}{2} \times t \times (v - u)$.

Since $v - u = at$: **$S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2$**.

slides.heading: Derivation 3: S = ½(u + v)t and v² = u² + 2aS
slides.body_md:
The area is a trapezoid: **$S = \dfrac{1}{2}(u + v)t$**.

Replace $t$ by $\dfrac{v - u}{a}$: $S = \dfrac{(u + v)(v - u)}{2a}$, so **$v^2 = u^2 + 2aS$**.

slides.heading: Which equation to use
slides.body_md: Choose the equation that contains the **three known** quantities and the **one unknown**. Take the direction of motion as positive; retardation has a negative sign.

visual.alt: Table of the four equations of motion and the quantity each one does not contain

slides.narration: Each equation leaves out one quantity. If the question does not mention time, use the fourth equation. If it does not mention the final velocity, use the second. Pick the equation that matches what you know.

slides.heading: Quick check: choosing an equation
slides.body_md: Find the equation with no time in it.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a car speeds up
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A car moving at 5 m s⁻¹ accelerates uniformly at 2 m s⁻² for 8 s. Find its final velocity and the distance covered.

**Step 1.** $v = u + at = 5 + 2 \times 8 = 21$ m s⁻¹.

**Step 2.** $S = ut + \dfrac{1}{2}at^2 = 5 \times 8 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 64 = 40 + 64 = 104$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the data and answers for the accelerating car

slides.narration: List what is given. Use the first equation for the final velocity, which is twenty one metres per second. Use the second equation for the distance, forty plus sixty four, which is one hundred and four metres.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: stopping distance
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A car at 20 m s⁻¹ brakes with a retardation of 5 m s⁻². Find the time and the distance before it stops.

**Step 1.** $v = 0$, $u = 20$, $a = -5$. $t = \dfrac{v - u}{a} = \dfrac{0 - 20}{-5} = 4$ s.

**Step 2.** $v^2 = u^2 + 2aS$ gives $0 = 400 - 10S$, so $S = \dfrac{400}{10} = 40$ m.

visual.alt: Table of the data and answers for the braking car

slides.narration: Retardation is a negative acceleration, so a is minus five. The car stops in four seconds. Since time was not asked for the distance, use the equation without time, which gives forty metres.

slides.heading: Quick check: braking
slides.body_md: The final velocity is zero when the body stops.

visual.alt: Table giving the data for a braking car

slides.narration: A car moving at ten metres per second brakes with a retardation of two point five metres per second squared. How far does it travel before it stops?

slides.heading: Free fall
slides.body_md: A body that falls only under gravity is in **free fall**. Near the Earth’s surface all bodies fall with the **same acceleration g**. In this chapter **g = 10 m s⁻²** (some books use 9.8). For a body dropped from rest, u = 0 and S = ½gt².

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a dropped stone
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A stone is dropped from a bridge 45 m above a river. Find the time to reach the water and its speed on arrival. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** $u = 0$, $a = g = 10$. $S = \dfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ gives $45 = 5t^2$, so $t^2 = 9$ and $t = 3$ s.

**Step 2.** $v = u + gt = 0 + 10 \times 3 = 30$ m s⁻¹.

visual.alt: Table of the data and answers for the dropped stone

slides.narration: A dropped body starts from rest. Put the height into the second equation to get the time, three seconds. Then the first equation gives the speed, thirty metres per second.

slides.heading: A body thrown vertically upward
slides.body_md: Going up, the velocity **falls** by 10 m s⁻¹ every second (a = −g). At the **highest point v = 0** but the acceleration is still g **downward**. The body returns to the starting level with the **same speed** it was thrown with, after twice the time taken to rise.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a ball thrown upward
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A ball is thrown vertically upward at 20 m s⁻¹. Find the time to the highest point, the maximum height and the total time of flight. (g = 10 m s⁻²)

**Step 1.** At the top $v = 0$: $0 = 20 - 10t$, so $t = 2$ s.

**Step 2.** $0 = 20^2 - 2 \times 10 \times S$, so $S = \dfrac{400}{20} = 20$ m.

**Step 3.** Time of flight $= 2 \times 2 = 4$ s.

slides.narration: Take upward as positive, so a is minus ten. At the top the velocity is zero, which gives two seconds. The fourth equation gives the height, twenty metres. The return takes as long as the rise, so the flight lasts four seconds.

notes.title: Motion in One Dimension — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Scalars, vectors, distance and displacement
sections.body_md:
A **scalar** quantity has only magnitude (distance, speed, mass, time). A **vector** has magnitude **and direction** (displacement, velocity, acceleration, force).

A body is **at rest** if its position does not change with time, and **in motion** if it does. Rest and motion are relative to a reference point.

- **Distance** is the total length of the path travelled; it is a scalar and is never negative.
- **Displacement** is the shortest distance from the initial to the final position, with the direction from start to end; it is a vector.

A school bus that goes 8 km north and 3 km back south covers a distance of 11 km, but its displacement is 5 km north. For a body moving along a straight line without turning back, the magnitude of the displacement equals the distance. When a body returns to its starting point the displacement is zero.

key_terms.definition_md: The total length of the path travelled by a body (scalar).
The shortest distance between the initial and final positions, in the direction from initial to final position (vector).

sections.heading: 2. Speed, velocity and acceleration
sections.body_md:
**Speed** = distance ÷ time (scalar); **velocity** = displacement ÷ time (vector). The SI unit of both is m s⁻¹.

- **Uniform motion:** equal distances in equal intervals of time (however small); the speed is constant.
- **Variable motion:** unequal distances in equal intervals.
- **Average speed** = total distance ÷ total time (do not average the speeds). A rider who covers 900 m in 180 s and 1500 m in 420 s has an average speed of 2400 ÷ 600 = 4 m s⁻¹.

**Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) ÷ t; SI unit m s⁻². A body speeding up has positive acceleration. If the velocity decreases, a is negative: this is **retardation** (deceleration). A train from rest to 30 m s⁻¹ in 120 s has a = 0.25 m s⁻².

Motion with **non-uniform acceleration** is outside this course; only uniform acceleration is studied. A body can move with constant speed but changing velocity (for example round a circle), because the direction changes.

key_terms.definition_md: Motion in which a body covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.
The rate of change of velocity of a body.
Negative acceleration: the rate at which the velocity of a body decreases.

sections.heading: 4. Equations of uniformly accelerated motion
sections.body_md:
For a body with initial velocity u, uniform acceleration a, final velocity v after time t and displacement S:

1. **v = u + at**
2. **S = ut + ½at²**
3. **S = ½(u + v)t**
4. **v² = u² + 2aS**

**Graphical derivation.** On the v–t graph the slope is a = (v − u) ÷ t, which gives (1). The area under the line is S: a rectangle ut plus a triangle ½ t (v − u) = ½ a t², which gives (2). The whole area is a trapezoid ½(u + v)t, which gives (3). Putting t = (v − u) ÷ a in (3) gives (4).

**Using the equations.** Pick the equation that contains the three known quantities and the unknown. Take the direction of motion as positive. A body that stops has v = 0 and a is negative.

Example: u = 5 m s⁻¹, a = 2 m s⁻², t = 8 s gives v = 21 m s⁻¹ and S = 104 m. A car at 20 m s⁻¹ with retardation 5 m s⁻² stops in 4 s after 40 m.

The equations hold only for **uniform** acceleration.

key_terms.definition_md: Motion in which the velocity changes by equal amounts in equal intervals of time.

sections.heading: 5. Motion under gravity
sections.body_md:
A body that moves only under the force of gravity is in **free fall**. In the absence of air resistance, all bodies fall with the same acceleration **g**, directed downward. In this chapter **g = 10 m s⁻²** (the value 9.8 m s⁻² is also used in books; a question will state the value).

**Dropped body** (u = 0, a = +g with downward positive): v = gt, S = ½gt², v² = 2gS. A stone dropped from 45 m takes 3 s and reaches the ground at 30 m s⁻¹.

**Body thrown upward** (take upward as positive, a = −g): the velocity falls by 10 m s⁻¹ every second; at the highest point **v = 0** but the acceleration is still g downward. Time to the top = u ÷ g; maximum height = u² ÷ 2g; the body returns to the starting level with the same speed after twice the time taken to rise. For u = 20 m s⁻¹: 2 s to rise, 20 m high, 4 s in the air.

key_terms.definition_md: The motion of a body under gravity alone, with no air resistance.
The acceleration g of a freely falling body; taken as 10 m s⁻² in this chapter.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Giving the distance when displacement is asked (or the other way round), and leaving out the direction of a vector.
- Averaging two speeds instead of using total distance ÷ total time.
- Forgetting to convert km per hour to m per second or minutes to seconds.
- Dropping the negative sign of a retardation, or using g = +10 for a body thrown upward with upward positive.
- Using the equations of motion when the acceleration is not constant.
- Reading the slope of a velocity-time graph as speed (it is acceleration), or taking the area under a distance-time graph as displacement (only the velocity-time area gives it).
- Forgetting that v = 0 at the highest point of a throw but the acceleration is still g.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a definition, a unit or one reading from a graph.
- 2 marks: a numerical with the formula, substitution and unit.
- 3 marks: a short derivation or a calculation in two steps.
- 10-mark structured question: parts on a graph or a free-fall situation: label the axes, show every substitution and give units; for a graphical derivation draw the graph and mark u, v, t and the areas.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The displacement of a body can be zero even when the distance travelled by it is not zero.

**Reason (R):** Displacement depends only on the initial and final positions of the body.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: If the body returns to its starting point the two positions coincide, so the displacement is zero; (R) explains (A), option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? The distance travelled by a body that has moved can be zero.
questions.solution_md: False. Distance is the length of the path and is positive for any motion; only the displacement can be zero.

questions.stem_md: Define displacement.

answer.model_answer_md: The **shortest distance between the initial and final positions of a body, in the direction from the first to the second**.

questions.solution_md: Shortest distance from start to end, with direction.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish a scalar quantity from a vector quantity, with one example of each.

answer.model_answer_md: A scalar has **magnitude only** (for example mass); a vector has **magnitude and direction** (for example force).

questions.solution_md: Magnitude only against magnitude and direction.

questions.stem_md: A girl completes one lap of a circular track of circumference 200 m in 50 s. Find her average speed and average velocity for the lap.

answer.model_answer_md: Average speed = 200 ÷ 50 = **4 m s⁻¹**. She returns to the starting point, so the displacement is zero and the average velocity is **zero**.

questions.solution_md: 4 m/s; zero.

questions.stem_md: A ferry crosses a river 150 m wide in 100 s and returns to the same bank in another 100 s. Its average velocity for the round trip is
questions.solution_md: The ferry ends where it started, so the displacement and hence the average velocity are zero; its average speed is 1.5 m s⁻¹, option (c).

questions.stem_md: A car goes round a circular track at a steady speed of 15 m s⁻¹. Its velocity

options.text_md: keeps changing because its direction keeps changing
is constant because its speed is constant
is zero because it returns to the start
is 15 m s⁻¹ in one fixed direction

questions.solution_md: Velocity is a vector; a change of direction is a change of velocity even at constant speed, option (a).

questions.stem_md: A body is said to have retardation when
questions.solution_md: Retardation is a negative acceleration: the velocity falls with time, option (b).

questions.stem_md: A car slows down from 20 m s⁻¹ to 5 m s⁻¹ in 5 s. Its acceleration is
questions.solution_md: $a = \dfrac{5 - 20}{5} = -3$ m s⁻² (a retardation of 3 m s⁻²), option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A car moving round a circular track with constant speed has constant velocity.

**Reason (R):** Velocity is a vector and changes when the direction of motion changes.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The direction keeps changing, so the velocity is not constant: (A) is false; (R) is true, option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Retardation is a negative acceleration.

**Reason (R):** A body moving with uniform velocity has zero acceleration.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both statements are true, but the second does not explain the first, option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A body moving with a constant velocity has zero acceleration.
questions.solution_md: True. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, which is zero if the velocity does not change.

questions.stem_md: A body that covers equal distances in equal intervals of time is said to move with ___ speed.
questions.solution_md: Uniform (constant) speed.

questions.stem_md: State the SI unit in which the area under a velocity-time graph is measured.

answer.model_answer_md: The **metre** (m), since the area is a displacement.

questions.solution_md: Metre.

questions.stem_md: A cyclist covers 480 m in 60 s and then 720 m in 180 s. Find the average speed for the whole journey in m s⁻¹.
A bus increases its speed from 6 m s⁻¹ to 21 m s⁻¹ in 10 s. Find its acceleration in m s⁻².
A bike moving at 14 m s⁻¹ is brought to rest uniformly in 7 s. Find its retardation in m s⁻².
questions.solution_md: $a = \dfrac{0 - 14}{7} = -2$ m s⁻², so the retardation $= 2$ m s⁻².

questions.stem_md: What is meant by retardation? Give one everyday situation in which it occurs.

answer.model_answer_md: Retardation is a **negative acceleration**: the velocity of the body **decreases** with time. For example, a car slowing down when the brakes are applied.

questions.solution_md: Velocity decreases; a braking car.

questions.stem_md: A girl jogs 200 m east in 50 s and then turns round and jogs 100 m west in 50 s. Find (a) her average speed and (b) her average velocity for the whole jog.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Distance = 200 + 100 = 300 m; time = 100 s; average speed = 300 ÷ 100 = **3 m s⁻¹**.

**(b)** Displacement = 200 − 100 = 100 m east; average velocity = 100 ÷ 100 = **1 m s⁻¹ towards east**.

questions.solution_md: 3 m/s; 1 m/s east.

questions.stem_md: State three differences between speed and velocity.

answer.model_answer_md:
**1.** Speed is the distance covered per unit time; velocity is the **displacement** per unit time.

**2.** Speed is a **scalar**; velocity is a **vector**.

**3.** Speed is **never negative or zero for a moving body** while velocity can be **zero or negative** (for example for a body that returns to its start).

questions.solution_md: Distance against displacement; scalar against vector; sign and zero values.

questions.stem_md:
The figure shows the velocity-time graph of a body moving with uniform acceleration a. The velocity is u at A at the start and v at B after time t, C is the foot of B on the time axis, D is level with B on the velocity axis and E is the origin.

(a) Using the slope of AB, derive v = u + at. [3]

(b) Name the figure whose area gives the displacement S in time t. [1]

(c) Using this area, derive S = ut + ½at². [3]

(d) A car starts at 4 m s⁻¹ and accelerates uniformly at 1.5 m s⁻² for 6 s. Find S. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The slope of AB is the acceleration: a = (v − u) ÷ t, so **v − u = at**, that is **v = u + at**.

**(b)** The **trapezium EABC**.

**(c)** Area = ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × width = ½ (u + v) t. Put v = u + at: S = ½ (2u + at) t = **ut + ½at²**.

**(d)** S = 4 × 6 + ½ × 1.5 × 36 = 24 + 27 = **51 m**.

questions.solution_md: a = (v − u)/t; trapezium EABC; ½(u + v)t with v = u + at; 51 m.

A truck moving at 30 m s⁻¹ on a straight road is brought to rest by its brakes, which give a uniform retardation of 5 m s⁻².

(a) State the value of the acceleration, with its sign, to be used in the equations of motion. [1]

(b) Find the time taken to stop. [2]

(c) Find the stopping distance using v² = u² + 2aS. [3]

(d) Find the average velocity during the stop and use it to check the stopping distance. [2]

(e) Describe the velocity-time graph of the truck during the stop and say what its area gives. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **a = −5 m s⁻²**.

**(b)** v = u + at: 0 = 30 − 5t, so t = **6 s**.

**(c)** 0 = 30² + 2 × (−5) × S, so S = 900 ÷ 10 = **90 m**.

**(d)** Average velocity = (30 + 0) ÷ 2 = **15 m s⁻¹**; distance = 15 × 6 = **90 m**, which agrees.

**(e)** A **straight line sloping down** from 30 m s⁻¹ at t = 0 to zero at t = 6 s; the **area** under it (a triangle) gives the **stopping distance**.

questions.solution_md: −5 m/s²; 6 s; 90 m; 15 m/s and 90 m; falling straight line, area is the distance.

questions.stem_md:
A boy standing on level ground throws a stone vertically upward at 30 m s⁻¹. Take g = 10 m s⁻² and neglect air resistance.

(a) Find the time taken to reach the highest point. [2]

(b) Find the maximum height reached. [3]

(c) Find the velocity of the stone 4 s after it is thrown, with its direction. [2]

(d) Find the total time for which the stone is in the air. [2]

(e) State the acceleration of the stone at the highest point. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** At the top v = 0: 0 = 30 − 10t, so t = **3 s**.

**(b)** 0 = 30² − 2 × 10 × H, so H = 900 ÷ 20 = **45 m**.

**(c)** v = u − gt = 30 − 10 × 4 = **-10 m s⁻¹**, that is **10 m s⁻¹ downward**.

**(d)** Total time = 2 × 3 = **6 s**.

**(e)** **10 m s⁻² downward** (the acceleration due to gravity).

questions.solution_md: 3 s; 45 m; 10 m/s downward; 6 s; 10 m/s² downward.

(d) Find the distance fallen in the first second and in the second second. [2]

(e) A stone and a feather are released together in a long vacuum tube. State what is observed and why. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** The motion of a body **under the force of gravity alone**.

**(b)** S = ½gt² = ½ × 10 × 2² = **20 m**.

**(c)** v = gt = 10 × 2 = **20 m s⁻¹** downward.

**(d)** First second: ½ × 10 × 1² = **5 m**; in the first 2 s: 20 m, so in the second second: 20 − 5 = **15 m**.

**(e)** They reach the bottom **together**, because without air resistance **both fall with the same acceleration g**.
